lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Every place on Earth has its own amazing story. Today, we follow the Sun Compass across the sea. Our little boat sails into Harbor Town on the Island of Fire. Fishing boats float in the harbor, and seagulls fly over the roofs. Behind the town stands a tall, green mountain. A little white steam rises from the top. Kiko asks, What is that mountain? A little red salamander in a yellow helmet waves from the pier. Welcome! I'm Ember, the island's junior safety ranger. That's Mount Cinder. That mountain is a volcano. Say it with me. That mountain is a volcano. Great! Riko looks a little worried. A volcano? Is it safe? Ember smiles. Don't worry. Mount Cinder is calm today, and scientists watch it every day. Then he gives us a lantern with six dark windows. This is the Safety Lantern. When you learn how to stay safe, a window will light up. Safety first, fun always! Let's read the sign at the harbor. "Welcome to the Island of Fire! Mount Cinder is a volcano. Its last eruption was about 300 years ago. Today, only a little white steam comes out of the top. Scientists at the Volcano Watch Center check the mountain day and night. Thanks to the volcano, our island has hot springs, rich soil, and beautiful views. Please enjoy your stay, and learn with us how to be safe and ready!" When was the last eruption? About 300 years ago. Who watches the mountain? Scientists at the Volcano Watch Center. Now, phonics. Rupt means break or burst. E means out. E plus rupt is erupt. To erupt means to burst out. Eruption is the noun. The last eruption was a long time ago. Erupted is the past. Mount Cinder erupted about 300 years ago, and now it's resting quietly. Next time, we will visit the Earth Science Museum and meet a volcano scientist!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That mountain is a volcano. Today, Ember takes us to the Earth Science Museum. In the main hall, there is a giant model of the earth. One part is cut open, like a slice of cake. A kind woman in a white coat walks over. Hello! I'm Dr. Mori. I'm a volcano scientist. I work here and at the Volcano Watch Center. She points to the colorful stripes inside the model. The earth isn't the same all the way through. The earth is made of layers. Say it with me. The earth is made of layers. Great! Haru shouts, Wow! What's in the middle? Then he covers his mouth. Oops, sorry for interrupting! Dr. Mori laughs. That's OK. Good questions are always welcome! Let's read the museum panel. "The Layers of the Earth. The earth is made of four layers. The outside layer is the crust. We live on the crust. It is very thin, like the skin of an apple. Under the crust is the mantle. It is very hot and very thick. Next comes the outer core. The inner core is in the very center. It is about as hot as the surface of the sun!" Which layer do we live on? The crust. How hot is the inner core? About as hot as the surface of the sun. Ember says, I love hot water, but that's too hot even for me! Now, phonics. Rupt means break. Inter means between. Inter plus rupt is interrupt. When you interrupt, you break into someone's talk. Interruption is the noun. Sorry for the interruption. Please go on. Interrupted is the past. Haru interrupted Dr. Mori, but he said sorry right away. How polite! Next time, we will make a model volcano erupt in the museum's science room!

On the table, there is a small clay mountain with a hole on top. Dr. Mori explains. Deep under a volcano, there is magma. Magma is melted rock under the ground. First, put the cup inside the top of the volcano. Next, put two spoons of baking soda into the cup. Then, add a few drops of red coloring. Finally, pour in the vinegar slowly and step back. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When a volcano erupts, hot lava comes out. Today, Ember takes us to his favorite place, the island hot springs. Warm steam rises from a big stone pool. We sit down and put our feet in the water. Ahh! Kiko asks, Why is the water hot? Ember says, It's heated deep underground. Volcanoes aren't only about lava. They give us presents, too! Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Say it with me. Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Great! Haru looks surprised. New islands? Ember nods. Yes! The islands of Hawaii were made by volcanoes. Let's read the board next to the hot springs. "Gifts from Our Volcano. Mount Cinder gives the island many gifts. Water is heated deep underground, so we can enjoy warm hot springs. Long ago, ash from the volcano fell on the land. Old ash makes the soil rich, so farmers grow sweet potatoes and many other vegetables here. Heat from deep underground can also make electricity. This is called geothermal energy. Volcanoes even make new islands, like the islands of Hawaii." Why is the soil rich? Because of old ash from the volcano. What is geothermal energy? Energy that comes from the heat underground. Suddenly, Ember jumps up. Oh! My tail is getting too warm! He gets out of the water very quickly, and everyone laughs. Now, phonics. Rupt means break. Ab means away. Ab plus rupt is abrupt. Abrupt means very sudden. Ember made an abrupt jump. Abruptly means suddenly. Ember got out of the water abruptly! Rupture means a break or a burst, like a rupture in a water pipe. Next time, we will share everything we learned at the Earth Science Show!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Volcanoes make hot springs and new islands. Today is the Earth Science Show at the museum! Dr. Mori, Ember, and many island children sit in the audience. Kiko talks about the layers of the earth. Haru explains magma and lava with our model volcano. Then it's Riko's turn. She holds up a big map of the world. The crust is broken into huge pieces called plates. They are always moving, but very, very slowly. The earth's crust moves slowly. Say it with me. The earth's crust moves slowly. Great! Let's read Riko's poster. "The Moving Plates. The earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called plates. Plates move only a few centimeters a year. That is about as fast as your fingernails grow! Japan is where four plates meet, so Japan has many earthquakes and volcanoes. In fact, Japan has about 111 active volcanoes. Mount Cinder is one of them, and scientists on our island watch it every day." How fast do plates move? About as fast as your fingernails grow. How many plates meet in Japan? Four. Everyone claps. Then Ember holds up the Safety Lantern. Look! One of the six windows is glowing with a warm orange light. You learned how the earth works. That's the first step to staying safe! Now, phonics. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What should you do during a typhoon? Today, Ember meets us at the Earth Science Museum with a big, empty backpack. He taps his yellow helmet and says, Safety first, fun always! Today, we will pack an emergency kit. An emergency kit is a bag of things you need when something big happens, like an earthquake or a typhoon. Riko asks, What goes inside? Ember smiles. The most important things come first. An emergency kit has water, food, and a flashlight. Say it with me. An emergency kit has water, food, and a flashlight. Great! Haru picks up a big bottle of water. Wow, this is heavy! Ember nods. Water is heavy, but we need a lot of it. Let's read Ember's checklist. "My Emergency Kit Checklist. Water: about three liters for each person for one day. Keep enough for at least three days. Food that keeps for a long time, like crackers and canned food. A flashlight and extra batteries. A radio, so you can hear the news. A first-aid kit for small cuts. A whistle, masks, gloves, and a warm jacket. Put copies of important papers in a waterproof bag. Check your kit often!" How much water does one person need for one day? About three liters. Why do we need a radio? So we can hear the news. Kiko packs the crackers and the canned food. Birimo tries on the gloves and waves his hands. Look, I'm ready for anything! Ember laughs. Don't forget the whistle, Birimo! Now, phonics. Proof means protects against, or strong against. Water plus proof is waterproof. A waterproof bag keeps the rain out. Wind plus proof is windproof. A windproof jacket keeps out the cold wind. Leak plus proof is leakproof. A leakproof bottle never drips, so your kit stays dry. Remember, we write each one as one word, with no space. Next time, we will visit a special safety house and look for the exits!

Ember says, Moving out of the building is like a slow parade. Slow, quiet, and in a line. If everyone hurries, people can bump into each other and fall. Haru asks, So what's the secret? Ember smiles. Stay calm. Follow your teacher. Say it with me. Stay calm. Follow your teacher. Wonderful! Then Ember writes four rules on the board. Schools in Japan have a special word for these rules, osahashimo. Let's read them. "Four Rules for Moving Out. One, don't push. Leave space between you and the person in front of you, so nobody falls. Two, don't run. Walk quickly, but carefully. Three, don't talk. Listen for your teacher's instructions. Four, don't go back. Leave your things behind, even your favorite pencil case. Never use the elevator. Use the stairs and follow your teacher." Why shouldn't we talk? Because we need to hear the teacher. What should you do with your things? Leave them behind. Kiko practices walking down the stairs slowly, holding the handrail. Birimo whispers, I'm playing a quiet turtle! Ember laughs softly. Perfect, Birimo. Slow and steady! Now, phonics. When we ask about A or B, the voice goes up on A and down on B. Is it an earthquake, up, or a typhoon, down? Should we go up, voice up, or stay here, voice down? Is the exit on the left, up, or on the right, down? lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When the ground shakes, get under a desk. If you hear a warning, go to high ground. Make sure your kit is ready. Today is the World 33 Safety Festival in the island square! Flags hang between the trees, and our posters are on every wall. Dr. Mori runs the volcano stand, and Grandma Tomo hands out warm rice balls. Then Ember climbs onto a box and holds up the Safety Lantern. He says, On this island, we learned three big things. Know it, prepare for it, and help each other. Say it with me. Know it, prepare for it, and help each other. Wonderful! Let's read the festival program. "Welcome to the World 33 Safety Festival! At the volcano stand, learn why Mount Cinder gives us hot springs. At the kit stand, pack a bag with water, food, and a flashlight. At the drill stand, practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On. At the helper stand, practice kind words in English and Japanese. Don't miss the poster corner! Thank you for keeping the Island of Fire safe and strong!" Where can you pack a bag? At the kit stand. What can you practice at the helper stand? Kind words in English and Japanese. Suddenly, the Safety Lantern shines brighter than ever. The sixth window lights up! Congratulations! All six windows are shining! A beam of light points over the hills to the small island airport. A little plane is waiting on the runway. Ember says, That plane flies to the Airport of Wings! Now, phonics. Let's review. Eruption. Rupt means burst. Emergency. Emerge, drop the last e, and add e, n, c, y. Earthquake-proof. Don't forget the hyphen. Drop, cover, and hold on. Drop, up. Cover, up. And hold on, down. Subject. Sub means under, and ject means throw. Goodbye, Ember! Goodbye, Dr. Mori and Grandma Tomo! See you at the Airport of Wings!
